# Classically integrable defects {#sec-defect-conditions}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Write down the general first-order defect Lagrangian and its defect conditions, and see why energy is always conserved while momentum is a strong constraint.
- Derive the conditions for a conserved modified momentum, and show that under the type-I ansatz they single out $a_r^{(1)}$ with the defect matrix $\mathsf D=2(1-\pi)^{-1}$.
- Construct the defect matrix $L_d(\lambda)$ that intertwines the Lax pairs on the two sides, and use it to see that charges of both chiralities survive, which corrects the literature.
- Derive the Poisson brackets of the defect values from the action, and show that $L_d$ satisfies the Sklyanin bracket with the bulk r-matrix, so that the defect charges are in involution.
- Recognize the defect conditions as a frozen Bäcklund transformation, and the delay of an $a_r$ soliton as its Bianchi coefficient.
- Know the type-II defects with an auxiliary field, the Tzitzéica defect, and the defects obtained by folding.
- Decide when a defect respects the antilinear symmetry $\Theta$.
:::

@sec-defect-sine-gordon treated the jump defect of sine-Gordon theory. This chapter asks which affine Toda theories admit such defects, and why the ones that do are integrable. The answer is more restrictive than for boundaries. Every affine Toda theory has integrable boundary conditions (@tbl-durham), but a defect that couples the two half-lines through first-order conditions, with no degrees of freedom of its own, exists only for $a_r^{(1)}$ [@bcz2004b; @cz2009a]. The criterion is momentum conservation: a defect breaks translation invariance, and asking for a modified momentum to survive leads to the same conditions as the existence of a Lax pair. Other algebras need a defect with an auxiliary field, the type-II defects of Corrigan and Zambon [@cz2009b], and these are known only case by case.

The chapter mirrors @sec-boundary-conditions. A Lagrangian and its conditions come first, then the criterion that selects the integrable ones, the Lax matrix, and the r-matrix structure. Two results are new. Both chiralities of conserved charges survive a type-I defect, which contradicts the literature (@prp-spin-two). And with the Poisson bracket that the defect term in the action induces on the defect values, the defect matrix satisfies the Sklyanin bracket with exactly the bulk r-matrix (@prp-defect-involution). Everything is classical. The solutions are the subject of @sec-defect-solitons and the quantum theory that of @sec-defect-qg.

## The defect Lagrangian {#sec-defect-lagrangian}

The field is $\vec\phi$ on $x<0$ and $\vec\psi$ on $x>0$, each with the bulk Lagrangian $\mathcal L$ of @sec-lagrangians and its potential $V$ (-@eq-imaginary-potential). A defect at $x=0$ that is linear in time derivatives and contains no derivatives in $x$ has the action [@bcz2004b, eq. (3.1)]

$$
S=\int dt\,\Big\{\int_{-\infty}^0\mathcal L(\vec\phi)\,dx+\int_0^\infty\mathcal L(\vec\psi)\,dx+\Big[\tfrac12\vec\phi\cdot E\,\partial_t\vec\phi+\vec\phi\cdot\mathsf D\,\partial_t\vec\psi+\tfrac12\vec\psi\cdot F\,\partial_t\vec\psi-\mathcal B_d(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)\Big]_{x=0}\Big\},
$$ {#eq-defect-action}

with constant real matrices $E$, $F$ (antisymmetric, since symmetric parts are total derivatives) and $\mathsf D$, and a **defect potential** $\mathcal B_d$. The bulk boundary terms of the variation are $-\partial_x\vec\phi\cdot\delta\vec\phi$ from $x<0$ and $+\partial_x\vec\psi\cdot\delta\vec\psi$ from $x>0$, and the **defect conditions** are

$$
\partial_x\vec\phi=E\,\partial_t\vec\phi+\mathsf D\,\partial_t\vec\psi-\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d,\qquad
\partial_x\vec\psi=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\partial_t\vec\phi-F\,\partial_t\vec\psi+\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d\qquad\text{at }x=0 .
$$ {#eq-defect-conditions}

The fields need not be continuous at $x=0$; this is a **jump defect**. Energy is always conserved. The bulk energy changes by $[\partial_t\vec\phi\cdot\partial_x\vec\phi-\partial_t\vec\psi\cdot\partial_x\vec\psi]_{x=0}$, and with (-@eq-defect-conditions) the terms quadratic in velocities cancel because $E$, $F$ are antisymmetric and the coefficient of $\partial_t\vec\psi$ in the first condition is the transpose of that of $\partial_t\vec\phi$ in the second. What remains is $-\frac d{dt}\mathcal B_d$, so $E+\mathcal B_d$ is conserved for every $\mathcal B_d$ (@exr-dc-energy). Corrigan and Zambon showed that these matrix properties are also necessary if the conditions are to conserve a modified energy [@cz2009a, eq. (2.6)].

**The type-I defects of $a_r^{(1)}$.** @sec-defect-momentum shows that a modified momentum is conserved only if, after a rotation of $\vec\psi$, $F=E=1-\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$, and that this requires $a_r^{(1)}$. Label the affine roots cyclically, $\vec\alpha_j=e_j-e_{j+1}$ in $\mathbb R^h$ ($j$ mod $h=r+1$), let $\vec\lambda_i$ ($i=1,\dots,r$) be the fundamental weights, with $\vec\lambda_0=\vec\lambda_{r+1}=0$, and let $\pi$ be the rotation of the diagram, $\pi\vec\alpha_j=\vec\alpha_{j-1}$. (The arrow distinguishes the weights from the spectral parameter $\lambda$.) Then

$$
\mathsf D=2\sum_{i=1}^r(\vec\lambda_i-\vec\lambda_{i+1})\vec\lambda_i^{\mathsf T}=2(1-\pi)^{-1},\qquad
E=F=1-\mathsf D=\sum_{i=1}^r\big(\vec\lambda_{i+1}\vec\lambda_i^{\mathsf T}-\vec\lambda_i\vec\lambda_{i+1}^{\mathsf T}\big),
$$ {#eq-d-matrix}

with $\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=2\delta_{ij}-2\delta_{i,j+1}$ and $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_j=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_{j-1}$ [@bcz2004b, eqs. (3.27)–(3.30)]. On the eigenvector of $\pi$ with eigenvalue $e^{2\pi ik/h}$, $k=1,\dots,r$, the matrix $\mathsf D$ is the number $2/(1-e^{2\pi ik/h})=1+i\cot\frac{\pi k}h$ (@exr-dc-d-matrix). For $a_1^{(1)}$, $\mathsf D=1$ and $E=0$, which is (-@eq-sg-defect-lagrangian). The **defect potential** is

$$
\mathcal B_d=\frac m{b^2}\sum_{j=0}^r\Big[\sigma\,(f_j-1)+\sigma^{-1}(g_j-1)\Big],\qquad
f_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi)/2},\quad g_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\mathsf D(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2},
$$ {#eq-defect-potential}

with $b=\beta$ at real and $b=i\beta$ at imaginary coupling, so that $\mathcal B_d^{\rm imag}$ follows from $\mathcal B_d^{\rm real}$ by $\beta\to i\beta$, as $V$ and the boundary potential do [@bcz2004b, eq. (3.32)] [@cz2007, eq. (2.10)]. The parameter is $\sigma=e^{-\theta_d}$, with $\theta_d$ the **defect rapidity** of @sec-sg-defect-lagrangian. This is the defect of **type I$_-$**, the one of Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon. Its time reverse, **type I$_+$**, has $(\mathsf D,E)\to(-\mathsf D,-E)$ and $\sigma\leftrightarrow\sigma^{-1}$ in $\mathcal B_d$, with $\mathsf D$ in $f_j,g_j$ unchanged. The identities $f_jg_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}$ and $f_jg_{j+1}=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\psi}$, consequences of $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_{j+1}=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j$, are what make the defect integrable. All of this is checked in `textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`.

**Other first-order defects.** Bristow and Bowcock wrote down the most general first-order defect Lagrangian with auxiliary fields $\vec\lambda(t)$ that live only at $x=0$: kinetic terms $\frac12\vec u\cdot A\vec u_t+\frac12\vec v\cdot B\vec v_t+\vec u\cdot C\vec v_t+\frac12\vec\lambda\cdot W\vec\lambda_t+\vec\lambda\cdot X\vec u_t+\vec\lambda\cdot Y\vec v_t$ and a potential $F(\vec u,\vec v,\vec\lambda)$ [@bristow_bowcock2017, eq. (2.6)]. Field redefinitions reduce every such defect that conserves momentum to components coupled as in type I and components coupled through auxiliary fields as in the type-II defects of @sec-type-two-atft.

**The literature.** @tbl-defect-dictionary translates the conventions of the sources.

## Momentum conservation as a criterion {#sec-defect-momentum}

The defect breaks translation invariance, so momentum is conserved only if the defect can absorb it. Corrigan and Zambon turned this into a criterion that is easier to use than the spin-3 charge of @prp-sg-defect-classification [@cz2009a]. With $P=-\int_{-\infty}^0\partial_t\vec\phi\cdot\partial_x\vec\phi\,dx-\int_0^\infty\partial_t\vec\psi\cdot\partial_x\vec\psi\,dx$ and the bulk field equations,

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=\Big[\tfrac12(\partial_t\vec\psi)^2+\tfrac12(\partial_x\vec\psi)^2-V(\vec\psi)-\tfrac12(\partial_t\vec\phi)^2-\tfrac12(\partial_x\vec\phi)^2+V(\vec\phi)\Big]_{x=0}.
$$ {#eq-dc-momentum-flux}

Substitute (-@eq-defect-conditions). The result is a polynomial of degree two in the velocities, and $P+P_d$ is conserved for a function $P_d(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ exactly when the three parts match separately.

::: {#prp-defect-momentum}
**[Established; numerically checked]** For the defect conditions (-@eq-defect-conditions), $P+P_d$ is conserved if and only if

1. (quadratic terms) $\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=1-E^2$, $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\mathsf D=1-F^2$ and $E\mathsf D=\mathsf DF$;
2. (linear terms) $\nabla_{\vec\phi}P_d=E\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d-\mathsf D\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d$ and $\nabla_{\vec\psi}P_d=-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d-F\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d$;
3. (no velocities) $\frac12\lvert\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d\rvert^2-\frac12\lvert\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d\rvert^2=V(\vec\phi)-V(\vec\psi)$.

Condition 1 holds exactly when $\mathsf D=(1-E)O$ and $F=O^{\mathsf T}EO$ with $O$ orthogonal; after the rotation $\vec\psi\to O\vec\psi$ it becomes $\mathsf D=1-E$, $F=E$. For the $a_r^{(1)}$ defect (-@eq-d-matrix), (-@eq-defect-potential) of either type all three hold, with
$$
P_d^{\rm I_-}=-\frac m{b^2}\sum_{j=0}^r\Big[\sigma(f_j-1)-\sigma^{-1}(g_j-1)\Big],\qquad P_d^{\rm I_+}(\sigma)=-P_d^{\rm I_-}(1/\sigma).
$$
In light-cone form, $E+P$ (spin $+1$) acquires only the $\sigma^{-1}g_j$ terms and $E-P$ only the $\sigma f_j$ terms.
:::

::: {.proof}
The three parts of $\frac d{dt}(P+P_d)$ are those listed [@cz2009a, eqs. (2.7)–(2.9)], rewritten for the book's sign of $P$ and with $F$ in place of their $-D$. Since $E$ is real antisymmetric, $1-E$ is invertible and $\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=(1-E)(1-E)^{\mathsf T}$ gives $O=(1-E)^{-1}\mathsf D$ orthogonal; then $E\mathsf D=\mathsf DF$ forces $F=O^{\mathsf T}EO$, and the second equation follows. For (-@eq-defect-potential), condition 3 follows from $f_jg_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}$ and $f_jg_{j+1}=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\psi}$: the cross terms of the squares give $\frac{m^2}{b^2}\sum_jf_j(g_j-g_{j+1})$, and the squares of the $f$ and $g$ terms cancel separately because $\mathsf D$ is normal. Condition 2 holds with the stated $P_d$ term by term: $E\mathsf D-\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=-\mathsf D$ for the $f_j$ and $E+\mathsf D=1$ for the $g_j$. All three conditions, the gradient form of condition 2, and the conservation laws along the defect conditions are checked at random complex points for $r=1,\dots,4$, both couplings and both types (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`).
:::

**The exponential ansatz.** The bulk potentials are sums of exponentials, so Corrigan and Zambon took $\mathcal B_d$ to be a finite sum of exponentials $e^{\vec a\cdot\vec\phi+\vec b\cdot\vec\psi}$, with $\mathsf D=1-E$ and $F=E$ [@cz2009a, eqs. (2.16)–(2.21)]. Condition 2 requires the vector field on its right-hand side to be a gradient, and this allows only two kinds of exponential: $f_{\vec x}=e^{b\vec x\cdot(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi)/2}$ and $g_{\vec y}=e^{b\vec y\cdot(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2}$. In condition 3 the squares of the $f$ terms and of the $g$ terms cancel, and a product $f_{\vec x}g_{\vec y}$ appears with the coefficient $\frac{b^2}2\vec x\cdot\vec y$ times the product of the two coefficients. It is a bulk exponential $e^{b\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\phi}$ only if $\vec x=\vec\alpha$, $\vec y=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha$, and $e^{b\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\psi}$ only if $\vec x=\vec\alpha$, $\vec y=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha$. Assume, as Corrigan and Zambon do, that the same affine Toda theory sits on both sides with the same roots after the rotation that set $\mathsf D=1-E$. Then the $f$ exponents are the roots $\vec\alpha_j$, and every unwanted product must have $\vec x\cdot\vec y=0$.

One more step makes this a statement about automorphisms. If some $\vec y=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i$ had no partner among the $-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_k$, it would have to be orthogonal to every $\vec\alpha_j$ with $j\ne i$, hence, since $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_j=0$, to $\vec\alpha_i$ as well, contradicting $\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i=\vec\alpha_i^2$. So there is a fixed-point-free permutation $p$ of the nodes with $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_{p(i)}$, that is $\mathsf D(\vec\alpha_i-\vec\alpha_{p(i)})=2\vec\alpha_i$. The linear map $P:\vec\alpha_i\mapsto\vec\alpha_{p(i)}$ exists because $\mathsf D$ is invertible, it is orthogonal because $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$, so $p$ is an automorphism of the affine Dynkin diagram, and

$$
\mathsf D=2(1-P)^{-1},\qquad\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=0\quad\text{for }j\notin\{i,p(i)\}
$$

[@bcz2004b, eqs. (3.19)–(3.24)]. Each $p$-orbit of nodes carries one free parameter. The second condition is the strong one, and it can be tested diagram by diagram.

::: {#prp-ar-only}
**[Established under the type-I ansatz; Numerical scan]** Under the assumptions just stated (constant real matrices, the same theory and the same roots on both sides after the rotation, and $\mathcal B_d$ a finite sum of exponentials), a modified momentum is conserved only for $a_r^{(1)}$, with $P=\pi$ or $\pi^{-1}$. Then $\mathcal B_d$ is (-@eq-defect-potential), or its mirror image with $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2(1-\pi^{-1})^{-1}$, which is the same defect after relabelling $j\to-j$. For every affine Dynkin diagram of rank at most 4, untwisted and twisted, and every one of its automorphisms, the scan confirms this: only $\pi^{\pm1}$ of $a_r^{(1)}$ pass.
:::

::: {.proof}
A short argument does most of the work. If $p$ has more than one orbit, then for each orbit $O$ the vector $\sum_{j\in O}\vec\alpha_j$ is fixed by $P$, and it is nonzero because the only linear relation among the affine roots, $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_j=0$, involves all of them with positive coefficients. So $1-P$ is singular, and $p$ must be a single cycle through all nodes. A tree has a centre, a node or an edge fixed by every automorphism, so the only affine diagrams with such an automorphism are the cycle $a_r^{(1)}$, $r\ge2$, and the two equal nodes of $a_1^{(1)}$; $p$ is then $\pi^k$ with $k$ coprime to $h$. Corrigan and Zambon show that the partner $p(i)$ must be a neighbour of $i$ [@cz2009a, eqs. (2.30)–(2.35)], which leaves $k=\pm1$. The scan in `textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py` confirms this without the argument. It runs through 23 diagrams ($a_1^{(1)},\dots,a_4^{(1)}$, $b_3^{(1)}$, $b_4^{(1)}$, $c_2^{(1)},\dots,c_4^{(1)}$, $d_4^{(1)}$, $f_4^{(1)}$, $g_2^{(1)}$, $a_2^{(2)}$, $a_4^{(2)}$, $a_6^{(2)}$, $a_8^{(2)}$, $a_3^{(2)}=d_3^{(2)}$, $a_5^{(2)}$, $a_7^{(2)}$, $d_4^{(2)}$, $d_5^{(2)}$, $e_6^{(2)}$, $d_4^{(3)}$) and their 78 automorphisms. In 64 cases $p$ fixes a node. In 5 cases $1-P$ is singular: the two reflections of $a_3^{(1)}$ that fix no node, the rotation $\pi^2$ of $a_3^{(1)}$, and the reversals of $c_3^{(1)}$ and $d_4^{(2)}$. The rotations $\pi^{\pm2}$ of $a_4^{(1)}$ produce ten forbidden cross terms each, and leave a residual of order 1 in condition 3. The remaining 7 automorphisms, $\pi^{\pm1}$ of $a_r^{(1)}$, $r=2,3,4$, and the exchange of the two nodes of $a_1^{(1)}$, pass, and condition 3 then holds at random points to $10^{-15}$.
:::

Two features of the answer stand out. Every other affine Toda theory, including the folded ones whose solitons are images of $a_r^{(1)}$ solitons, has no type-I defect. And the obstruction is combinatorial: the defect matrix must come from an automorphism that cycles through all the nodes, and a potential without unwanted cross terms then needs the cycle to be the diagram itself. Corrigan and Zambon also found that a defect may join different theories, because conformal Toda theory has no affine root: an $a_r$ conformal Toda theory on the left and an $a_{r-1}$ conformal Toda theory plus a free massless field on the right, so that $r$ defects in a row reduce conformal Toda theory to free fields [@cz2009a, eqs. (2.42)–(2.44)].

Is momentum conservation enough for integrability? For type I it is. @sec-defect-lax constructs a Lax pair for exactly these defects, and a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ admits none. For the type-II defects of @sec-type-two-atft, Bristow constructed defect Lax matrices for the Tzitzéica defect and for a $d_4^{(1)}$ defect, and in both cases momentum conservation was exactly what was needed [@bristow2017, Sec. 3].

::: {#cnj-momentum-integrability}
**[Conjecture]** A first-order defect in affine Toda theory, with or without auxiliary fields, is classically integrable, in the sense that it admits a defect Lax matrix and infinitely many conserved charges, if and only if it conserves a modified momentum.
:::

Bristow calls momentum conservation "very likely" necessary for integrability [@bristow2017, Sec. 3.4]. The evidence is the type-I classification, the $a_1$, Tzitzéica and $d_4$ Lax matrices, and the fact that every momentum-conserving defect found so far is a Bäcklund transformation when imposed for all $x$ [@bristow_bowcock2017, Sec. 3]. The analogy with boundaries is instructive. At a boundary the energy is always conserved, so energy conservation selects nothing, and integrability is the much stronger condition of @sec-durham-classification; at a defect the energy is also free, but momentum is a genuine constraint, and the conjecture says it is the only one. In the quantum theory the analogy may fail: Penati and Polvara found that a finite renormalization restores quantum momentum conservation but not the spin-3 charge [@penati_polvara2019, Sec. 5] (@cnj-defect-parameter).

## Lax pairs with a defect {#sec-defect-lax}

Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon constructed the Lax pair of the defect theory from two Lax pairs on overlapping regions, $x<b$ for $\vec\phi$ and $x>a$ for $\vec\psi$, related by a gauge transformation in the overlap [@bcz2004, Sec. 4] [@bcz2004b, Sec. 3]. Shrinking the overlap to the point $x=0$ leaves a single matrix. With $a_t=\frac12(\mathcal A_++\mathcal A_-)$ of (-@eq-boundary-lax-at), a solution $\Psi$ of $(\partial_t+a_t)\Psi=0$ on each side, and $\Psi_\phi=L_d\Psi_\psi$ at $x=0$, the **defect matrix** $L_d(\lambda)$ must satisfy

$$
\partial_tL_d=L_d\,a_t(\vec\psi)-a_t(\vec\phi)\,L_d\quad\text{at }x=0,\qquad
L_d(\lambda)=e^{-bH\cdot(E\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi)/2}\,\tilde L(\lambda)\,e^{bH\cdot(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi-E\vec\psi)/2},
$$ {#eq-defect-lax-matrix}

with the defect conditions used to eliminate $\partial_x\vec\phi$, $\partial_x\vec\psi$, and $\tilde L(\lambda)$ independent of the fields. In the defining representation of $a_r^{(1)}$, where $E_{\vec\alpha_j}=e_{j,j+1}$ (indices mod $h$) and $S=\sum_jE_{\vec\alpha_j}$ is the cyclic permutation matrix,

$$
\tilde L_{\rm I_-}(\lambda)=1+\frac\sigma\lambda\sum_{j=0}^rE_{-\vec\alpha_j}=1+\frac\sigma\lambda S^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\tilde L_{\rm I_+}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}\Big(\frac\lambda\sigma\Big)^kS^k\ \propto\ \Big(1-\frac\lambda\sigma S\Big)^{-1}.
$$

For type I$_-$ the defect matrix simplifies to $L_d=e^{bH\cdot(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2}\big[1+\frac\sigma\lambda\sum_je^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w/2}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big]$ with $\vec w=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi-E\vec\psi$: the Cartan factor sees only the jump $\vec\phi-\vec\psi$.

::: {#prp-defect-lax}
**[Established; numerically checked for $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$]** For the $a_r^{(1)}$ defects (-@eq-d-matrix), (-@eq-defect-potential), the matrix (-@eq-defect-lax-matrix) satisfies its evolution equation on the defect conditions, for both couplings. In the defining representation the field-independent $\tilde L$ is unique up to a scalar factor, with the coefficient of $\sigma/\lambda$ exactly 1 in the normalization of @sec-lax-pair; this is [@bcz2004b, eq. (3.39)] with their $d=\sigma$ and their $\lambda$ equal to the book's. For a $\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$ other than (-@eq-d-matrix) there is no field-independent $\tilde L$. On the vacuum, a soliton of rapidity $\theta$ corresponds to $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$, so the off-diagonal part $\sigma/\lambda$ of $\tilde L_{\rm I_-}$ grows like $e^{\theta-\theta_d}$, as the conversion amplitude of @sec-sg-defect-solitons does.
:::

::: {.proof}
Substituting (-@eq-defect-lax-matrix) and the defect conditions, the evolution equation becomes a Laurent polynomial in $\lambda$ whose coefficients are sums of exponentials of the fields. Order by order in $1/\lambda$ it determines $\tilde L$ and forces (-@eq-d-matrix) and (-@eq-defect-potential) [@bcz2004b, eqs. (3.9)–(3.39)]. We solved the linear equations for $\tilde L$ numerically, stacked over random field configurations, for $r=1,2,3$, both couplings and both types, and found a one-dimensional solution space with the stated $\tilde L$, and none for $E\to0.6E$ (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`).
:::

**Which charges survive.** Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon expected the "lack of balance between $\lambda$ and $1/\lambda$" in $\tilde L$ to distinguish the two chiralities, and concluded from the spin-$\pm2$ charges of $a_r^{(1)}$ that only one of them survives each type of defect [@bcz2004b, Sec. 5]; Penati and Polvara repeated the classical argument [@penati_polvara2019, App. B]. Their argument was that the terms cubic in velocities in the defect flux of the lost charge are proportional to $A_{abc}(\mathsf D_{ap}\mathsf D_{bq}\mathsf D_{cr}+\mathsf D_{pa}\mathsf D_{qb}\mathsf D_{rc})$ [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.11)], with $A_{abc}$ the cubic coefficients of the bulk spin-2 density, and that this does not vanish "because of (3.20)", the relation $\mathsf D=2-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$. That inference is wrong, and so is the conclusion.

::: {#prp-spin-two}
**[Numerical for $a_2$ and $a_3$; Proposition, sketch for all $a_r^{(1)}$]** For both types of defect, both the spin $+2$ and the spin $-2$ charges of $a_r^{(1)}$ survive, with local defect contributions. More generally, for every $s$ the bulk charges of spin $+s$ and of spin $-s$ both survive separately, each with a local defect contribution.

1. The obstruction of [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.11)] vanishes identically for every $r$.
2. The generating function $\tau_d(\lambda)$ of (-@eq-defect-monodromy) is conserved, and $L_d(\lambda)$, $L_d(\lambda)^{-1}$ have Laurent expansions with invertible leading coefficients both at $\lambda\to\infty$ and at $\lambda\to0$. Its expansions at the two ends give local charges of the two chiralities, each with a local defect contribution.
3. For $a_2^{(1)}$ the defect flux of each spin-$\pm2$ charge is a total time derivative, for both types, and the defect contributions $\mathcal B_{\pm2}$ are given explicitly in `textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`; for $a_3^{(1)}$ the same holds numerically.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1) The cubic invariant of $a_r$ is $A(\vec u,\vec u,\vec u)=\frac23\sum_{k=1}^h(\vec\mu_k\cdot\vec u)^3$, with $\vec\mu_k$ the weights of the defining representation; with $B=1-\mathsf D$ [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.6)] it solves their (5.5). Expand $\vec v$ in eigenvectors of $\pi$. The cubic invariant couples only modes with $k_1+k_2+k_3\equiv0$ mod $h$, and on them $\mathsf D=1+ic_i$ with $c_i=\cot\frac{\pi k_i}h$. The obstruction is a sum of terms $d_1d_2d_3+\bar d_1\bar d_2\bar d_3=2\big[1-(c_1c_2+c_2c_3+c_3c_1)\big]$, and $\cot a\cot b+\cot b\cot c+\cot c\cot a=1$ whenever $a+b+c\equiv0$ mod $\pi$ (@exr-dc-cot). So the obstruction vanishes, although each of its two terms does not. Polarization gives the same for the mixed cubic terms of [@penati_polvara2019, eq. (B.4)].

(2) The argument of @sec-conserved-charges applies on each half-line. At $\lambda\to\infty$ the Drinfeld–Sokolov gauge transformation $G(x;\lambda)$, a local series in $1/\lambda$, brings the transport matrices to $e^{-\int\mathfrak h\,dx}$ with $\mathfrak h$ in the principal Heisenberg subalgebra, whose coefficients are the bulk densities of one chirality [@drinfeld_sokolov1985; @olive1985]. Then $\tau_d=\operatorname{tr}\big(G^\psi(x_+)\,e^{-\int_0^{x_+}\mathfrak h^\psi}N(\lambda)\,e^{-\int_{x_-}^0\mathfrak h^\phi}G^\phi(x_-)^{-1}\big)$ with $N(\lambda)=G^\psi(0)^{-1}L_d(\lambda)^{-1}G^\phi(0)$, and for large $|\lambda|$ on a suitable ray one eigenvalue $k_*$ of $\mathfrak h$ dominates: $\ln\tau_d$ is the sum of the two bulk integrals and $\ln N_{k_*k_*}(\lambda)$. Since $L_d(\lambda)^{-1}$ tends to an invertible Cartan element, $N_{k_*k_*}$ has a nonzero leading term for generic defect values, and $\ln N_{k_*k_*}$ is a series in $1/\lambda$ whose coefficients are functions of $\vec\phi(0)$, $\vec\psi(0)$ and finitely many derivatives; the $x$-derivatives reduce to $t$-derivatives through the defect conditions and the field equations. At $\lambda\to0$ the same argument uses the opposite gauge, in which $\lambda^{-1}S^{\mathsf T}$ dominates. Now $\tilde L_{\rm I_-}=\frac\sigma\lambda S^{\mathsf T}(1+\frac\lambda\sigma S)$, and $S^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible, so after the scalar factor $\sigma/\lambda$ the leading coefficient of $L_d^{-1}$ is $S$ dressed by Cartan elements, whose diagonal entries in the eigenbasis of $S$ are again nonzero for generic defect values. For type I$_+$, $\tilde L_{\rm I_+}^{-1}\propto1-\frac\lambda\sigma S$ is regular at both ends in the same way. Nothing couples the two ends of the $\lambda$-plane, unlike the double-row matrix (-@eq-double-row) of a boundary, which contains both $T(\lambda)$ and $T(1/\lambda)$ and therefore only the combinations $Q_s+Q_{-s}$. The invertibility statements are checked in `textbook_code/defect_lax_rmatrix.py`. What is not proved here: control of the dominant eigenvalue on the infinite line, which is standard but not written out, and the reorganization of the expansion where the leading entry vanishes, which happens at imaginary coupling on special values of the jump. Hence the label "sketch".

(3) With the defect conditions, the flux of each charge through $x=0$ is a function of $\vec\phi(0,t)$, $\vec\psi(0,t)$ and their first three time derivatives. It is a total time derivative of a local function if and only if its Euler operator in $t$ vanishes, which we checked symbolically to $10^{-15}$, together with closed-loop integrals along random periodic paths. Controls: the spin-$\pm1$ fluxes pass, a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ fails, the bulk current is conserved on shell, and its density is not a total $x$-derivative. The homotopy formula then constructs $\mathcal B_{\pm2}$: both are linear in $\partial_t\vec\phi$, $\partial_t\vec\psi$ plus a sum of exponentials, and $\frac d{dt}\mathcal B_{\pm2}$ reproduces the flux to $10^{-15}$. For type I$_-$, $\mathcal B_{+2}$ contains the velocities only multiplied by $\sigma^{-1}g_j$ and $\mathcal B_{-2}$ only multiplied by $\sigma f_j$, as for $E\pm P$ in @prp-defect-momentum (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`). The $a_3^{(1)}$ case was run separately, at about six minutes per case, and is not part of the script.
:::

So the two types are not distinguished by which spin-$\pm2$ charge survives. They differ in the $\lambda$-dependence of $\tilde L$, in the Borel subalgebra of the quantum group that their quantum transmission matrices intertwine (@prp-two-borels), and, for sine-Gordon, in the direction of soliton conversion: type I$_-$ converts solitons faster than the defect, type I$_+$ slower ones (@prp-sg-delay). This is why the book names the types by their Borel subalgebra.

## The defect monodromy and the classical r-matrix {#sec-defect-r-matrix}

The transport matrix $T(x_+,x_-;\lambda)$ of @sec-sklyanin, with $\partial_{x_+}T=-a_x(x_+)T$, carries $\Psi$ from $x_-$ to $x_+$. A solution on the whole line crosses the defect by $\Psi_\psi=L_d^{-1}\Psi_\phi$, so the **defect monodromy** is

$$
\mathcal T_d(\lambda)=T_+(\lambda)\,L_d(\lambda)^{-1}\,T_-(\lambda),\qquad\tau_d(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda),
$$ {#eq-defect-monodromy}

with $T_+=T^\psi(x_+,0)$ and $T_-=T^\phi(0,x_-)$. The evolution equation of $L_d^{-1}$, $\partial_tL_d^{-1}=L_d^{-1}a_t(\vec\phi)-a_t(\vec\psi)L_d^{-1}$, is exactly what makes the boundary terms at $x=0$ cancel, and with fields that decay at $x_\pm\to\pm\infty$ the generating function $\tau_d(\lambda)$ is conserved [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.1)]. (They write the inverse matrix, transporting from right to left.)

**The Poisson structure of the defect values.** Integrability in the sense of Liouville also needs the charges to Poisson-commute. The defect term in (-@eq-defect-action) is first order in time derivatives, so it is a symplectic potential for the defect values $\vec z=(\vec\phi(0),\vec\psi(0))$. Up to a total time derivative it equals $\frac12\vec z\cdot K\partial_t\vec z$ with

$$
K=\begin{pmatrix}E&\mathsf D\\-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}&E\end{pmatrix},\qquad\{z_I,z_J\}=(K^{-1})_{IJ},
$$ {#eq-dc-defect-bracket}

in the convention $\{\phi_a(x),\pi_b(y)\}=\delta_{ab}\delta(x-y)$ of the bulk. For sine-Gordon $\{\phi(0),\psi(0)\}=-1$ for type I$_-$ and $+1$ for type I$_+$. Treating the defect term as a pair of second-class constraints, as Corrigan and Zambon do for sine-Gordon theory [@cz2009b, Sec. 6], gives the same Dirac bracket (by hand). The defect matrix is built from exponentials of linear functions of $\vec z$, so its bracket with itself is quadratic in $L_d$, and the question is whether it has the Sklyanin form.

::: {#prp-defect-involution}
**[Established; numerically checked]** Give the defect values the bracket (-@eq-dc-defect-bracket), Poisson-commuting with the bulk fields. Then, for $a_r^{(1)}$, both types and both couplings,
$$
\{L_d(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,L_d(\lambda_2)\}=\Big[r\Big(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\Big),\,L_d(\lambda_1)\otimes L_d(\lambda_2)\Big],
$$
with the r-matrix $r(z)$ of @prp-sklyanin ($\beta^2\to b^2$) and coefficient exactly 1. The bulk transport matrices satisfy $\{T(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,T(\lambda_2)\}=-[r,T(\lambda_1)\otimes T(\lambda_2)]$, so $L_d^{-1}$, and with it $\mathcal T_d$, satisfies the same quadratic relation as $T$, and $\{\tau_d(\lambda_1),\tau_d(\lambda_2)\}=0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The bracket of $L_d$ follows from (-@eq-dc-defect-bracket) by the chain rule. We compared it with $[r,L_d\otimes L_d]$ for $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, both types, both couplings and real and complex $\lambda_{1,2}$: the relative residual is $10^{-15}$ and the coefficient is $1$ to $10^{-15}$. A non-integrable $\mathsf D$ leaves a residual of 0.18 (`textbook_code/defect_lax_rmatrix.py`). For the bulk sign, the transport matrix over one lattice site of length $\Delta$, $T=e^{-\Delta a_x}$ with $\{\phi_a,\pi_b\}=\delta_{ab}/\Delta$, satisfies $\{T\overset\otimes,T\}=c\,[r,T\otimes T]$ with $c=-1+O(\Delta)$ (same script). If $\{L_1,L_2\}=[r,L_1L_2]$ then $\{L_1^{-1},L_2^{-1}\}=-[r,L_1^{-1}L_2^{-1}]$, so all three factors of $\mathcal T_d$ obey the same quadratic algebra, and their product does too, since the factors Poisson-commute. Then $\{\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda_1),\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda_2)\}=\mp\operatorname{tr}_{12}[r,\mathcal T_{d1}\mathcal T_{d2}]=0$. We checked the involution with random $T_\pm$ satisfying the bulk relation and the computed bracket of $L_d^{-1}$, to $10^{-14}$; it fails if $L_d$ replaces $L_d^{-1}$ in (-@eq-defect-monodromy), or if the defect bracket has the wrong sign (same script).
:::

The normalization is the point. The defect term was fixed in @sec-defect-momentum by momentum conservation, which knows nothing about Poisson brackets. That its symplectic form makes $L_d$ a classical $L$-operator for exactly the bulk r-matrix, with coefficient 1 and the right sign, is a strong consistency check, and it is the classical shadow of the quantum statement that the transmission matrix is an $L$-operator of a Borel subalgebra (@sec-t-intertwiner). Since the brackets of the linear functions $\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w$ and $\vec\phi-\vec\psi$ are constants, their exponentials form a Poisson algebra of Weyl type, the classical limit of the $q$-Weyl algebras behind the $q$-oscillator representations of the quantum theory.

**What the proposition does not settle.** The assumption that the defect values Poisson-commute with the bulk fields is the delicate step. The equal-time bracket of the field theory does not restrict to the boundary values of fields in a well-defined way, and the direct use of the r-matrix is hindered by divergences at the defect [@caudrelier2015, Sec. 1]. There are two ways around this. Habibullin and Kundu regularized the sine-Gordon defect on a lattice and derived its classical and quantum r-matrix structure and all its charges [@habibullin_kundu2008]. Avan and Doikou postulated a defect matrix satisfying the quadratic algebra, regarded its entries as independent degrees of freedom, and imposed "sewing conditions" with the bulk as constraints with Dirac brackets [@avan_doikou2012a; @avan_doikou2012b]; they reported discrepancies with the charges of the Lagrangian approach. Doikou extended the construction to $\mathfrak{gl}_N$ type-I defects in spin chains [@doikou2014]. Caudrelier resolved the tension differently [@caudrelier2008; @caudrelier2015; @caudrelier_kundu2015]. In a second, "time-like" Poisson bracket, in which $x$ plays the role of time, the sine-Gordon model is Hamiltonian with the same r-matrix, and the defect conditions are a canonical transformation. In the book's conventions this is immediate from the action: with $G[\vec\phi,\vec\psi]=\int dt\,\big[\frac12\vec\phi\cdot E\vec\phi_t+\vec\phi\cdot\mathsf D\vec\psi_t+\frac12\vec\psi\cdot E\vec\psi_t-\mathcal B_d\big]$, the conditions (-@eq-defect-conditions) read $\partial_x\vec\phi=\delta G/\delta\vec\phi(0,t)$ and $\partial_x\vec\psi=-\delta G/\delta\vec\psi(0,t)$, so the map from $(\vec\phi,-\partial_x\vec\phi)$ to $(\vec\psi,-\partial_x\vec\psi)$ on the line $x=0$ is generated by $-G$ [@caudrelier2015, Prop. 3.1]. Caudrelier then proved Liouville integrability of the sine-Gordon defect with the r-matrix in the time-like bracket [@caudrelier2015, Sec. 3.3]. For $a_r^{(1)}$ the same steps should go through, but we have not carried them out.

**Comparison with a boundary.** The boundary generating function $\tau(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}(K_+T(\lambda)K_-(1/\lambda)\sigma(T(1/\lambda)))$ of (-@eq-double-row) is built from one transport matrix and its image, and integrability requires the reflection equation (-@eq-classical-reflection) for the field-independent $K_\pm$. The defect generating function is built from two independent transport matrices and a field-dependent $L_d$, and integrability requires that $L_d$ itself be a representation of the bulk Poisson algebra. A defect pressed against a boundary therefore produces a field-dependent $K$-matrix, $K_+(\lambda)$ dressed by $L_d$, which is how the defect parameter becomes a boundary parameter in @sec-sg-breather-transmission and @sec-defect-boundary-fusion.

## Defect conditions as Bäcklund transformations {#sec-defect-backlund-an}

For sine-Gordon theory the defect conditions are a Bäcklund transformation frozen at $x=0$ (@sec-sg-defect-lagrangian). The same is true for $a_r^{(1)}$. Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon asked when conditions of the form (-@eq-defect-conditions), imposed for all $x$, are compatible with Lorentz-invariant field equations on both sides. Cross-differentiating gives $\partial_x^2\Psi=M^2\partial_t^2\Psi+\dots$ with $\Psi=(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ and $M=\begin{pmatrix}E&\mathsf D\\\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}&-F\end{pmatrix}$, and decoupled Lorentz-invariant equations require $M^2=1$, a condition on the second derivatives of $\mathcal B_d$, and condition 3 of @prp-defect-momentum [@bcz2004b, eqs. (5.19)–(5.25)]. Solving these reproduces (-@eq-d-matrix) and (-@eq-defect-potential) [@bcz2004b, eqs. (5.26)–(5.43)]. We checked directly that for $r=1,\dots,4$, both types and both couplings, cross-differentiation of the conditions gives both field equations, and that a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ does not (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`). Write $\vec\psi=\mathfrak B_\sigma\vec\phi$ for this Bäcklund transformation. For $a_2^{(1)}$ it is the Bäcklund transformation of Fordy and Gibbons, as Corrigan and Zambon observed [@cz2009b, Sec. 5].

**The delay is the Bianchi coefficient.** Send the soliton (-@eq-an-soliton) of species $a$ and rapidity $\theta$ through a type-I$_-$ defect at imaginary coupling, and look for $\vec\psi$ of the same form with $E\to z_aE$. The defect conditions hold for all $t$ exactly when

$$
z_a(\theta)=\frac{e^{-(\theta-\theta_d)}-ie^{i\pi a/h}}{e^{-(\theta-\theta_d)}-ie^{-i\pi a/h}}
=\frac{\mathsf a(\theta)+\varepsilon_a\,\mathsf a(\theta_d)}{\mathsf a(\theta)-\varepsilon_a^{-1}\mathsf a(\theta_d)},\qquad\mathsf a(\theta)=-e^{-\theta},\quad\varepsilon_a=e^{i\pi(2a-h)/2h},
$$ {#eq-dc-ar-delay}

which is [@cz2009a, eq. (4.10)], [@bcz2004b, eq. (6.2)] after $\theta\to-\theta$, and [@cz2007, eq. (2.20)] after $a\to h-a$, because their $\mathsf D$ is the book's $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$. The pair $(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ of full-line solutions satisfies the conditions not only at $x=0$ but at every $x$: it is a Bäcklund pair, $\vec\psi=\mathfrak B_\sigma\vec\phi$. So the delay is the factor by which $\mathfrak B_\sigma$ multiplies $E$, the $a_r$ version of the Bianchi coefficient of (-@eq-sgd-bianchi), and the second form of (-@eq-dc-ar-delay) displays it with the Bäcklund parameters $\mathsf a(\theta)$ of @prp-sg-backlund. For $h=2$, $\varepsilon_1=1$ and it reduces to $z_{\rm I_-}$ of (-@eq-sg-delay). For $h>2$ the coefficient is twisted by the phase $\varepsilon_a$, and $z_a$ is complex for real rapidities; the phase of $z_a$ is what moves the topological charge of a passing soliton to a neighbouring weight (@sec-an-soliton-defect). Two identities generalize those of @prp-half-soliton:

$$
z_a(\theta)\,z_{\bar a}(\theta)=\frac{\cosh(\theta-\theta_d)+\sin\frac{\pi a}h}{\cosh(\theta-\theta_d)-\sin\frac{\pi a}h},\qquad
z_{\bar a}(\bar\theta;\bar\theta_d)=\overline{z_a(\theta;\theta_d)},\qquad\bar a=h-a.
$$

For $h=2$ the first is $z^2=\coth^2\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2=1/A_{11}$. For self-conjugate solitons, $a=h/2$, $z_{h/2}=-\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2$ is the sine-Gordon delay, with the sign that converts solitons faster than the defect. We checked (-@eq-dc-ar-delay) by root-finding and at $x=0$, $-0.7$ and $1.3$ for $a_2^{(1)}$ (species 1 and 2), the self-conjugate soliton of $a_3^{(1)}$ and $a_1^{(1)}$, together with the dictionary to the three sources and the two identities (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`). @sec-defect-solitons develops the consequences: the selection rule for the topological charge, the absence of absorption at real rapidity except for self-conjugate solitons, and multi-soliton transmission.

## Type-II defects in affine Toda theory {#sec-type-two-atft}

@prp-ar-only leaves every theory except $a_r^{(1)}$ without a type-I defect. Corrigan and Zambon found a way out for the Tzitzéica theory $a_2^{(2)}$ by giving the defect a degree of freedom $\Lambda(t)$ of its own [@cz2009b]. For one field component the defect term is

$$
\Big[\tfrac12(\phi\,\partial_t\psi-\psi\,\partial_t\phi)+\Lambda\,\partial_t(\phi-\psi)-(\phi-\psi)\,\partial_t\Lambda-\mathcal D(\phi,\psi,\Lambda)\Big]_{x=0},
$$ {#eq-dc-type-two}

and the defect conditions are $\partial_x\phi=\partial_t\psi-2\partial_t\Lambda-\partial_\phi\mathcal D$, $\partial_x\psi=\partial_t\phi-2\partial_t\Lambda+\partial_\psi\mathcal D$ and $\partial_t\phi-\partial_t\psi=\frac12\partial_\Lambda\mathcal D$ [@cz2009b, eqs. (2.1)–(2.4)]. As for type I, $E+\mathcal D$ is conserved for every $\mathcal D$. With $p=\frac12(\phi+\psi)$ and $q=\frac12(\phi-\psi)$, a modified momentum exists exactly when $\mathcal D=f(q,p-\Lambda)+g(q,\Lambda)$ with

$$
\tfrac12\big(\partial_qf\,\partial_\Lambda g-\partial_\Lambda f\,\partial_qg\big)=V(\phi)-V(\psi),
$$

and then $P+g-f$ is conserved [@cz2009b, eqs. (2.10)–(2.12)]. The left-hand side is the Poisson bracket of $f$ and $g$ with $\Lambda$ and $-2q$ as conjugate variables. This condition replaces condition 3 of @prp-defect-momentum. It is still strong, since all dependence on $\Lambda$ must cancel, but it admits the Tzitzéica potential, which condition 3 excludes [@cz2009b, Sec. 2].

::: {#prp-type-ii-momentum}
**[Established; numerically checked for sine-Gordon and Tzitzéica]** For the sine-Gordon defect [@cz2009b, eq. (3.2)] and the Tzitzéica defect [@cz2009b, eq. (3.7)], $E+\mathcal D$ and $P+g-f$ are conserved, and a soliton passes with a pure delay. For sine-Gordon the delay is $\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2$ or its inverse, depending on the sector of $\Lambda$; for Tzitzéica it is one of three delays whose product is 1.
:::

::: {.proof}
The conservation laws were checked at random complex points along the defect conditions, and the solitons by solving the two conditions without $\partial_t\Lambda$ for $e^{\hat\lambda}$ at each time and checking the third with a numerical derivative, to $10^{-7}$ (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`), in the variables described next.
:::

**Sine-Gordon.** In the rescaled variables of Corrigan and Zambon, $\hat p=\beta_{\rm SG}p$, $\hat q=\beta_{\rm SG}q$, $\hat\lambda=\beta_{\rm SG}\Lambda$ and $\hat x=m_0x/\sqrt2$ for sinh-Gordon, the defect potential is $\mathcal D=\frac{m_0}{\sqrt2\,\beta_{\rm SG}^2}(f+g)$ with

$$
f=\frac1{\hat\sigma}\Big[2e^{\hat p-\hat\lambda}+e^{-\hat p+\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}+2\cosh2\tau\big)\Big],\qquad
g=\hat\sigma\Big[e^{\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}+2\cosh2\tau\big)+2e^{-\hat\lambda}\Big],
$$

and $\hat\sigma=e^{\theta_d}$ (their $\sigma=e^\eta$); sine-Gordon follows by $\beta_{\rm SG}\to i\beta_{\rm SG}$. The two parameters are the defect rapidity $\theta_d$ and $\tau$. With no jump, the vacuum has $e^{2\hat\lambda}=1/(2\cosh^2\tau)$ [@cz2009b, eq. (3.4)], and the two square roots give two sectors. If $e^{\hat\lambda}\to+1/(\sqrt2\cosh\tau)$ before the soliton arrives, the delay is

$$
z=\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2\,\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2=z_{\rm I_-}(\theta;\theta_d+\tau)\,z_{\rm I_-}(\theta;\theta_d-\tau),
$$

the delay of two type-I$_-$ defects at rapidities $\theta_d\pm\tau$ without jumps. If $e^{\hat\lambda}\to-1/(\sqrt2\cosh\tau)$, that is $\hat\lambda\to\hat\lambda+i\pi$, the delay is its inverse, $\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2$, the product of two odd-sector delays $z_{\rm odd}=-\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2$ of @sec-sg-defect-solitons. This is the sector that Corrigan and Zambon call $z_1$ [@cz2009b, eq. (4.3)]. In that sector $e^{\hat\lambda}=-\frac1{\sqrt2\cosh\tau}\,\frac{(1+E_0)(1+zE_0)}{(1-\rho E_0)(1-\tilde\rho E_0)}$ with $E_0=E(0,t)$, $\rho=\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2$, $\tilde\rho=\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2$; their (4.4) has the opposite overall sign and $+\rho$, $+\tilde\rho$ in the denominator, and does not satisfy the defect conditions. The type-II defect is the fused pair of two type-I defects (@sec-type-two), and $\hat\lambda$ remembers the field between them.

**Tzitzéica.** In the book's normalization the $a_2^{(2)}$ theory has roots $\sqrt2$ (long, label 1) and $-1/\sqrt2$ (short, label 2), so $V_{\rm real}=\frac{m^2}{\beta^2}\big(e^{\sqrt2\beta\phi}+2e^{-\beta\phi/\sqrt2}-3\big)$ and the particle has mass$^2$ $3m^2$. Corrigan and Zambon's field is $u=\beta\phi/\sqrt2=\beta_{\rm lit}\phi$, with the coupling $\beta_{\rm lit}^2=\beta^2/2$ of the normalization in which the long root has length$^2$ 4 (@sec-conventions), and $\hat x=mx/\sqrt2$. Their defect potential is $\mathcal D=\frac{\sqrt2m}{\beta^2}(f+g)$ with

$$
f=\frac1{\hat\sigma}\Big[e^{2\hat p-2\hat\lambda}+e^{-\hat p+\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}\big)\Big],\qquad
g=\frac{\hat\sigma}2\Big[8e^{-\hat\lambda}+e^{2\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}\big)^2\Big],
$$

where $\hat p$, $\hat q$, $\hat\lambda$ are $\beta_{\rm lit}$ times $p$, $q$, $\Lambda$, and the factor $1/\hat\sigma$ multiplies both terms of $f$, as the defect conditions [@cz2009b, eq. (4.6)] and the momentum condition require. There is one parameter, and with $e^{\theta_d}=\sqrt2\hat\sigma$ the three delays are

$$
z_1=\coth\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2-\frac{i\pi}{12}\Big)\coth\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2+\frac{i\pi}{12}\Big),\qquad
z_{2,3}=\coth\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2\mp\frac{i\pi}4\Big)\tanh\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2\pm\frac{i\pi}{12}\Big),
$$

with $z_1z_2z_3=1$ and $z_3=\bar z_2$ for real rapidities [@cz2009b, eqs. (4.9)–(4.11)]. The sector is fixed by the asymptotic value of $e^{\hat\lambda}$, which is $1$, $e^{-2\pi i/3}$ and $e^{2\pi i/3}$ respectively. (Their (4.11) lists $z_3$ under the name $z_2$; the set of delays is unaffected.) These were the first integrable defects of a theory outside $a_r^{(1)}$. Corrigan and Zambon also obtained the Tzitzéica conditions by folding two "squeezed" $a_2^{(1)}$ defects, of opposite rotations [@cz2009b, Sec. 5], gave the type-II defects of $a_n^{(1)}$ as fused pairs of the two rotations [@cz2011, eq. (2.6)], and computed the Tzitzéica transmission matrix [@cz2011, Sec. 3], which @sec-a22-transmission takes up.

**Beyond.** Bristow and Bowcock found momentum-conserving type-II defects for $a_n^{(1)}$, $b_n^{(1)}$, $c_n^{(1)}$ and $d_n^{(1)}$ [@bristow_bowcock2017, Sec. 4]; their potentials (4.19), (4.23), (4.27), (4.30) identify these as the untwisted algebras, with Kac labels $1,1,2,\dots,2,1,1$ for $d_n^{(1)}$ and $1,2,\dots,2,1$ for $c_n^{(1)}$. Their $a_n^{(1)}$ defect is the fused pair of two type-I defects. They computed soliton delays through the $d_4^{(1)}$ defect, and Bristow constructed defect Lax matrices for the Tzitzéica and $d_4^{(1)}$ defects [@bristow2017, Secs. 3.3–3.4]. We know of no defect for $e_6^{(1)}$, $e_7^{(1)}$ and $e_8^{(1)}$. We have not checked these results.

## Folding defects {#sec-defect-folding}

Folding gives non-simply-laced theories from simply-laced ones (@sec-affine-folding), and Robertson applied it to defects [@robertson2014a]. A type-I defect of $a_r^{(1)}$ cannot be folded directly. The reflection of the diagram that folding uses maps $\pi$ to $\pi^{-1}$, hence $\mathsf D$ to $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$, so it maps a defect to its mirror image. A fused pair of a defect and its mirror image, a type-II defect of $a_r^{(1)}$ [@cz2011], is invariant, and its folding gives defects of three series:

- $a_{2n-1}^{(1)}\to c_n^{(1)}$, by the reflection that fixes nodes $0$ and $n$, the canonical folding of @tbl-foldings;
- $a_{2n}^{(1)}\to a_{2n}^{(2)}$, by the reflection $j\to-j$ that fixes node $0$, the first construction of @sec-affine-folding;
- $a_{2n-1}^{(1)}\to d_n^{(2)}$, by the fixed-point-free reflection $j\to1-j$, whose orbits $\{0,1\}$ and $\{n,n+1\}$ consist of adjacent roots and give the short end nodes. This parent is not the one in @tbl-foldings ($d_{n+1}^{(1)}$); the folded roots must be rescaled by $\sqrt2$, and space and time by $1/\sqrt2$, to reach the standard normalization [@robertson2014a, Sec. 2].

Momentum conservation in the folded theory forces the two parameters of the pair to be equal up to sign. Opposite signs give no defect at all, the second defect annihilating the first; equal signs give a genuine defect, through which folded solitons pass with a delay [@robertson2014a, Sec. 3]. For $c_2^{(1)}$ the result agrees with the defect found by Bristow and Bowcock directly. These defects are not type I, consistent with @prp-ar-only, and Robertson notes that they need not be the only ones. The folding of solitons is the same as on the half-line (@sec-images-cn), where $c_n$ solitons are invariant $a_{2n-1}$ solitons. In a sequel Robertson introduced fusing rules for $a_r^{(1)}$ defects, classically and quantum mechanically, and used them to build a new $a_3^{(1)}$ transmission matrix [@robertson2014b]. We have not re-derived these results.

## Reality and the defect {#sec-defect-theta}

In the bulk the antilinear map $\Theta:\vec\phi\mapsto-\bar{\vec\phi}$ maps solutions of the imaginary-coupling theory to solutions (@sec-theta-classical). @prp-boundary-theta showed that a boundary respects it exactly when its parameters are real. For a defect, $\Theta$ acts on both fields.

::: {#prp-defect-theta}
**[Theorem]** For both types of $a_r^{(1)}$ defect at imaginary coupling,
$$
\overline{\mathcal B_d(\vec\phi,\vec\psi;\sigma)}=\mathcal B_d(-\bar{\vec\phi},-\bar{\vec\psi};\bar\sigma)
$$
for all complex fields. Hence $\Theta:(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)\mapsto(-\bar{\vec\phi},-\bar{\vec\psi})$ maps solutions of the defect theory with parameter $\sigma$ to solutions with parameter $\bar\sigma$, and it is a symmetry if and only if $\sigma$ is real, that is $\theta_d\in\mathbb R+i\pi\mathbb Z$. Then $E+\mathcal B_d$ and $P+P_d$ of $\Theta\vec\phi$ are the complex conjugates of those of $\vec\phi$. At real coupling the same holds for plain complex conjugation, the form $\Theta$ takes there (@exr-theta-solutions).
:::

::: {.proof}
In $\mathcal B_d^{\rm imag}=-\frac m{\beta^2}\sum_j[\sigma(f_j-1)+\sigma^{-1}(g_j-1)]$ the matrices $\mathsf D$, $E$ are real, and conjugation sends $f_j(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ to $f_j(-\bar{\vec\phi},-\bar{\vec\psi})$ and likewise $g_j$. This gives the identity. Conjugating the defect conditions then shows that $\Theta$ of a solution with $\sigma$ solves them with $\bar\sigma$; the bulk is as in @sec-theta-classical. The functions $f_j-1$ and $g_j-1$ are linearly independent, so $\mathcal B_d(\cdot;\bar\sigma)=\mathcal B_d(\cdot;\sigma)$ only if $\bar\sigma=\sigma$. We checked the identity for $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_3^{(1)}$, both types and both couplings, and the action on an $a_2^{(1)}$ soliton passing a defect with complex $\sigma$: its $\Theta$-image satisfies the conditions with $\bar\sigma$ to $10^{-15}$ and violates them with $\sigma$ (`textbook_code/defect_classical_an.py`).
:::

On solitons, $\Theta$ maps $(a,\theta,\xi)$ to $(\bar a,\bar\theta,\bar\xi)$ (-@eq-theta-data), and the delays transform accordingly, $z_{\bar a}(\bar\theta;\bar\theta_d)=\overline{z_a(\theta;\theta_d)}$ (@sec-defect-backlund-an). For real $\theta_d$ a soliton and its antisoliton are delayed by complex conjugate factors, as Corrigan and Zambon noted [@cz2007, Sec. 2]. Real $\sigma$ includes the odd sector $\sigma\to-\sigma$ of sine-Gordon, $\theta_d\to\theta_d+i\pi$. Imaginary $\theta_d$, which @sec-sg-defect-spectrum needs for stable excited defects, breaks $\Theta$, as the Lee–Yang defects of @sec-defect-lee-yang do. The type-II potentials above have real coefficients when $\hat\sigma$ and $\cosh2\tau$ are real, and then $\Theta$, acting as complex conjugation on the rescaled fields and on $\hat\lambda$, is a symmetry (by hand). @sec-defect-reality uses @prp-defect-theta for the reality of the energies of solitons passing a defect.

## Exercises {#sec-defect-conditions-exercises}

::: {#exr-dc-energy}
Derive (-@eq-defect-conditions) from (-@eq-defect-action), and show that $E+\mathcal B_d$ is conserved for any $\mathcal B_d$. Conversely, start from conditions $\partial_x\vec\phi=A\partial_t\vec\phi+B\partial_t\vec\psi+\vec X$, $\partial_x\vec\psi=C\partial_t\vec\phi+D\partial_t\vec\psi+\vec Y$ with constant matrices, and show that a modified energy is conserved only if $C=B^{\mathsf T}$, $A$ and $D$ are antisymmetric, and $\vec X$, $\vec Y$ are gradients of one function [@cz2009a, eq. (2.6)].
:::

::: {#exr-dc-d-matrix}
Prove the properties of $\mathsf D$ listed after (-@eq-d-matrix): $\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=2(\vec\lambda_j-\vec\lambda_{j+1})$, $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$, $\mathsf D=2(1-\pi)^{-1}$, $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_j=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_{j-1}$, and $\mathsf D=1+i\cot\frac{\pi k}h$ on the eigenvectors of $\pi$. Show that $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2(1-\pi^{-1})^{-1}$, and that the reflection $\vec\alpha_j\to\vec\alpha_{-j}$ of the diagram conjugates $\mathsf D$ into $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$. Deduce that a soliton of species $a$ passing the mirror defect is delayed as a soliton of species $h-a$ passing the original one.
:::

::: {#exr-dc-scan}
Carry out the scan of @prp-ar-only by hand for small diagrams. (a) Show that every automorphism of $d_4^{(1)}$, $b_n^{(1)}$ and the twisted algebras of rank 2 fixes a node. (b) For $c_3^{(1)}$, show that the reversal of the chain fixes no node but fixes the vector $\vec\alpha_0+\vec\alpha_3$, so that $1-P$ is singular. Generalize: an automorphism with more than one orbit never works. (c) For $a_4^{(1)}$ and $P=\pi^2$, compute $\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j$ and find the forbidden cross terms. (d) For $a_1^{(1)}$, show that the exchange of the two nodes gives $\mathsf D=1$ and (-@eq-sg-defect-potential).
:::

::: {#exr-dc-cot}
Prove $\cot a\cot b+\cot b\cot c+\cot c\cot a=1$ for $a+b+c\equiv0$ mod $\pi$. Show that $A(\vec u,\vec u,\vec u)=\frac23\sum_k(\vec\mu_k\cdot\vec u)^3$ solves [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.5)] with $B=1-\mathsf D$, and that $A(\mathsf D\vec v)^3+A(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec v)^3=0$. For $a_2^{(1)}$ write out $A(\mathsf D\vec v)^3$ and check that it is not zero.
:::

::: {#exr-dc-lax}
For $a_1^{(1)}$ in the two-dimensional representation, with $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, verify that $L_d=e^{-bH\psi/2}(1+\frac\sigma\lambda\sigma_x)e^{bH\phi/2}$ satisfies $\partial_tL_d=L_da_t(\psi)-a_t(\phi)L_d$ on the defect conditions (-@eq-sg-defect-conditions). Using the boost property of @sec-lax-pair, show that the coefficients of $\lambda^{-n}$ at $\lambda\to\infty$ have spin $-n$ and those of $\lambda^n$ at $\lambda\to0$ spin $+n$. Show that the first defect contribution at $\lambda\to\infty$ is proportional to $\sigma$ and the first at $\lambda\to0$ to $\sigma^{-1}$, as for $E-P$ and $E+P$ in @prp-sg-defect-momentum.
:::

::: {#exr-dc-bracket}
For $a_1^{(1)}$, show from (-@eq-dc-defect-bracket) that $\{\phi(0),\psi(0)\}=-1$ for type I$_-$. Using $r(z)$ of @prp-sklyanin with $h=2$, verify $\{L_d(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,L_d(\lambda_2)\}=[r(\lambda_1/\lambda_2),L_d(\lambda_1)\otimes L_d(\lambda_2)]$ entry by entry. What changes for type I$_+$?
:::

::: {#exr-dc-delay}
For the $a_r$ soliton, show that $f_j=\tau_{j+1}\tau'_{j-1}/(\tau_j\tau'_j)$ and $g_j=\tau_{j-1}\tau'_j/(\tau_j\tau'_{j-1})$, where $\tau'_j$ are the $\tau$-functions of $\vec\psi$. Substitute into the defect conditions for $a_2^{(1)}$ and derive (-@eq-dc-ar-delay). Prove the twisted Bianchi form, the identity for $z_az_{\bar a}$, and $z_{\bar a}(\bar\theta;\bar\theta_d)=\overline{z_a(\theta;\theta_d)}$.
:::

::: {#exr-dc-type-two}
From (-@eq-dc-type-two) derive the type-II defect conditions and show that $E+\mathcal D$ is conserved. Verify that the sine-Gordon $f$ and $g$ satisfy $\frac12(f_qg_\Lambda-f_\Lambda g_q)=V(\phi)-V(\psi)$ in the rescaled variables, and find the static values of $e^{\hat\lambda}$ when the jump is even and when it is odd. Show that the two delays of @prp-type-ii-momentum are $z_{\rm I_-}(\theta;\theta_d+\tau)z_{\rm I_-}(\theta;\theta_d-\tau)$ and $z_{\rm odd}(\theta;\theta_d+\tau)z_{\rm odd}(\theta;\theta_d-\tau)$, and that they are inverse to each other.
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-defect-conditions-notes}

Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon introduced the Lagrangian jump defect for sine-Gordon theory and showed that its conditions are a frozen Bäcklund transformation [-@bcz2004]. They then extended it to affine Toda theory, constructed the defect matrix by overlapping Lax pairs, found that only $a_r^{(1)}$ admits a type-I defect, and recovered the defect from the Bäcklund condition [-@bcz2004b]. Corrigan and Zambon computed the delays of $a_r$ solitons and the $a_2$ transmission matrix [-@cz2007], made momentum conservation the organizing principle [-@cz2009a], introduced type-II defects with the Tzitzéica example [-@cz2009b], and related the defects to infinite-dimensional representations of Borel subalgebras [-@cz2011]. Robertson folded fused $a_r$ defects [-@robertson2014a] and introduced defect fusing rules [-@robertson2014b]. Bristow and Bowcock generalized type-II defects to several auxiliary fields and found them for four series of algebras [-@bristow_bowcock2017], and Bristow constructed their Lax matrices [-@bristow2017]. Habibullin and Kundu gave a lattice-regularized r-matrix treatment of the sine-Gordon defect [-@habibullin_kundu2008], Avan and Doikou the sewing-condition approach [-@avan_doikou2012a; -@avan_doikou2012b], Doikou its $\mathfrak{gl}_N$ version [-@doikou2014], and Caudrelier the systematic and multisymplectic treatments [-@caudrelier2008; -@caudrelier2015; -@caudrelier_kundu2015]. Penati and Polvara studied the quantum conservation laws [-@penati_polvara2019]. The scan of @prp-ar-only, the survival of both chiralities with the general cancellation and the explicit $\mathcal B_{\pm2}$ of @prp-spin-two, the bracket (-@eq-dc-defect-bracket) with the exact Sklyanin relation of @prp-defect-involution, the twisted Bianchi form (-@eq-dc-ar-delay), and @prp-defect-theta are stated here.

Corrections and clarifications to the sources made in this chapter:

- Both spin-$\pm2$ charges of $a_r^{(1)}$ survive a type-I defect of either type, contrary to [@bcz2004b, Sec. 5] and [@penati_polvara2019, App. B]. The obstruction [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.11)] vanishes identically: their inference from $\mathsf D=2-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$ [@bcz2004b, eq. (3.20)] to a nonzero (5.11) overlooks that the cubic invariant couples only Fourier modes with $k_1+k_2+k_3\equiv0$ mod $h$, on which the cotangent identity cancels the two terms. The cubic terms of [@penati_polvara2019, eq. (B.4)] vanish for the same reason. The two types differ in their Borel subalgebra, not in a surviving charge.
- In [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.43)] the matrix is printed as $2\sum_i\vec\lambda_i(\vec\lambda_i-\vec\lambda_{i+1})^{\mathsf T}$, the transpose of their (3.28); with their $E$ of (5.42), $1-E$ is the matrix of (3.28).
- [@cz2007, eq. (2.21)]: for a self-conjugate soliton their (2.20) gives $z=-\coth\frac{\theta-\eta}2$, not $+\coth\frac{\theta-\eta}2$; the sign is that of the sine-Gordon delay (-@eq-sg-delay) and of [@bcz2004b, eq. (6.2)].
- [@cz2009b, eq. (4.4)]: the defect field in the sector of the delay $z_1$ is $e^{\lambda_1}=-\frac1{\sqrt2\cosh\tau}\frac{(1+E_0)(1+z_1E_0)}{(1-\rho E_0)(1-\tilde\rho E_0)}$; the printed form, with the opposite overall sign and $1+\rho E_0$, $1+\tilde\rho E_0$, violates the defect conditions (3.3), and their (4.5) changes accordingly. Their $z_1$ is the sector $e^\lambda\to-1/(\sqrt2\cosh\tau)$.
- [@cz2009b, eq. (3.7)]: $1/\sigma$ multiplies both terms of $f$, as their (4.6) requires. Their (4.11) for $z_2$ is the complex conjugate of the $z_2$ of their (4.9), i.e. their $z_3$.
